articles.title_orig: Arcadia couple at center of surrogacy scandal have been arrested on multiple charges, Eyewitness News has learned
articles.title_zh: Arcadia couple at center of surrogacy scandal have been arrested on multiple charges, Eyewitness News has learned
articles.content_orig:
A California couple at the center of a surrogacy scandal was arrested on Tuesday. A law enforcement source confirmed the arrests to CBS News shortly before officials held a news conference to announce the latest developments.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang are being charged with multiple counts including conspiracy to commit child abuse and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said. He is asking for bail to be set at $100 million.
The couple drew national headlines last year after authorities raided their Arcadia mansion in July 2025 and took 21 kids, mostly surrogate-born , into state custody.
Tuesday morning, detectives from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department arrested the couple at their residence. They were transferred to the Pasadena courthouse where they are currently being arraigned, Sheriff Robert Luna said.
"What has been publicly filed in the complaint today is incredibly disturbing. It involves horrific punishment and beatings and child abuse," Hochman said at the news conference.
Melissa Brisman, an attorney for two of the surrogates involved in the case, told CBS News, "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system."
Brisman added that it's important surrogacy remains an option for those who need the help to become parents, but said there must "be adequate protections for those who enter the surrogacy system."
"We need to make sure bad actors don't ruin it for everyone else," she said.
A Los Angeles FBI spokesperson confirmed the FBI served a search warrant at the home, separate from a search conducted by the sheriff's department.
A neighbor said helicopters and police could be seen at their mansion and the entire block is taped off.
Officials said the investigation began in May 2025 when Zhang brought a 2-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury.
"She appeared to be untruthful with hospital staff about how the injury was sustained and the hospital staff notified law enforcement authorities," Luna said, adding that when Arcadia police went to the home, "what they discovered raised even more serious concerns."
In early September, the Arcadia Police Department requested assistance from the LA County Sheriff's Department.
"We will continue to work together to pursue justice for all 21 children involved in this case," Luna said.
Maria Castellanos, a surrogate who carried two children for Zhang and Xuan, said after learning of their arrest, "I'm mad that everyone involved couldn't stop this so the kids wouldn't go through everything they went through. I'm just mad with the whole process, the whole thing. It's not just them."
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Ex-C.I.A. Officer Who Stashed Gold Bars Admits to Far Larger $145 Million Scam
articles.title_zh: Ex-C.I.A. Officer Who Stashed Gold Bars Admits to Far Larger $145 Million Scam
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A former CIA official who was found with $40 million in gold bars in his home in May pleaded guilty on Tuesday, admitting he invented fake classified programs to divert nearly $200 million in government money that he used to buy Florida mansions and gold.
David Rush entered a guilty plea on a single count of wire fraud during a hearing in federal court in Virginia.
As part of his plea agreement , Rush agreed to forfeit at least $194 million, including 298 gold bars, two BMWs, 35 luxury watches and four luxury homes in Florida. He faces up to 20 years in prison.
In a filing known as a criminal information detailing the allegations Rush admitted to, prosecutors said he invented a fake classified program to steer $145 million in government funds through a front company, using the money to purchase the homes in Florida that he intended to resell for profit. Separately, he "fabricated a separate purported sensitive government activity to justify the acquisition of gold bars," prosecutors said.
"Although the real estate and gold acquisitions involved different transactions and intermediaries, they were executions of the same overarching scheme — RUSH created false classified authorities, directed and approved the associated expenditures, caused contractors and subcontractors to carry out the transactions, and thereafter exercised possession or control over the acquired assets," the filing said.
Prosecutors said Rush had access to "highly sensitive and classified government programs," although the filing does not name the CIA as his former employer. The spy agency and FBI said previously that the investigation began when the CIA referred the matter to the bureau. In the affidavit supporting the original criminal complaint against him, he was described as a "former Senior Executive Service level employee" at a government agency in eastern Virginia.
The document said Rush caused an unidentified contractor known as Company 1 to transfer about $145 million to a holding company set up at his direction. He then instructed employees at that company and a subcontractor to route that money to a holding company that he controlled, and used the funds to purchase four properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida.
Rush was arrested in May. FBI agents found the gold bars, $2 million in cash and luxury watches when executing a search warrant at his home. Prosecutors said Tuesday that the holding company had about $38.6 million left in its account.
The gold bars were purchased after Rush told the unnamed contractors "that he was working on a Top-Secret project in which he had to deliver high-value commodities to unnamed individuals," the information said. One of the contractors wired $45 million to the holding company in January, a transaction that forms the basis of the wire fraud charge.
Rush was originally charged with one count of stealing public money, with investigators saying he had provided false information about his education and military service on his government application, and fraudulently took military leave after his service ended.
In June, a federal judge ordered Rush to remain in custody as the case proceeded, determining that he posed a severe flight risk.
At his detention hearing, government lawyers called Rush a "master manipulator" who lied to his neighbors about being a pilot, lied to his co-workers and leveraged his "access to seniority." A Justice Department lawyer said Rush "cannot be trusted" and is "fully willing and able to skirt the rules."
Callie  Teitelbaum contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.title_zh: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.content_orig:
YANKTON, S.D. – Julie Jones won silver at the World Archery 3D Championships, and in doing so created history by becoming the first USA woman to win an individual medal at the event, which began in 2003.
Jones was making only her second-ever appearance at the World Archery 3D Championships. She was part of the women’s team including Jayme Buchanan, Katherine Li and Madison Ritter to claim bronze at the 2024 World 3D Championships in Mokrice, Slovenia. Two years on and she did even better.
“It's a little surreal, I'll be honest,” began Julie Jones on hearing she had made history. “I love 3D. That is my passion aside from hunting. I guess if you ask me how I felt about it, I'm glad that I could bring it back for the U.S. team. But it really isn't a short answer. It goes a lot further than that.
"This whole time that I've been shooting, I've had an incredible team of people behind me from the very beginning. They have encouraged, they've pushed, they've believed in me when I had doubts about my own abilities. Without them, none of none of this would have been possible.
“I know that I don't have to prove anything to them but bringing this silver medal home, it's a testament to the training and the coaching that that I've received, that this medal belongs to all of these people, not just to me.”
Jones was seeded seventh after qualification before moving through the bracket with wins over teammate Mandy Boggs, Olga Timofeeva (RUS) and Martina Blahusova (CZE). The U.S. archer from Texas settled for silver after defeat in the gold medal match to fifth seed Judith Wenzl (GER).
“I had 100 percent confidence in the training and the coaching that I'd received," explained Jones. "I knew that if I applied all of the mental work, all of the physical work, as well as the actual shooting, I was reasonably confident that I could be in the top 10. That really wasn't a doubt in my mind.
"I knew that if I ran my process and executed well, that there was a good chance I would be in the top five, if not the top three. So that part of it was not necessarily a surprise to me.
“I've had some health challenges along the way and so day two was not a good day for me physically. And it was a struggle just to make it through the round. So that kind of threw a spanner into it.
“But I'm glad that it worked out as well as it did. I shoot very well under pressure. And I knew that if I could make it into those head-to-head eliminations, that I could work. Even though I had dropped points on day two, I knew that I could work myself back up to a to a better position.”
Julie Jones was also part of the bronze medal-winning traditional mixed team alongside Cody Hasson. Hasson, a double gold medalist at last year’s Pan American Field Championships, finished sixth in the individual men’s event.
Jones added, “I am tickled to death that Cody and I ended up with the bronze medal. He is a really, really strong shooter. I may be mistaken, but I don't think he's ever medaled before (at World 3D), and just to see the excitement and the absolute joy on his and our coach Shiloh's (Butts) face, when we realized that we had won that last round, that was a great feeling.”
For Jones, this was a family affair, with husband Daniel having also made the team. For Daniel, it was not only his World 3D Championship debut but also his first major event outside of local competition. A first major event for Daniel and the first U.S. woman to win an individual medal at the World 3D Championships for Julie. A case of keeping up with the Joneses!
“I'm just a normal person,” continued Julie. “I'm a mom. I have kids. I'm self-employed. I don't have a big, fancy facility, but, you know, I go out and I'm passionate about 3D archery.”
This success comes just a few weeks before a significant birthday for Julie on November 1. She said with a smile, “Just a month before, to achieve this, I couldn’t ask for anything more. This is year 50 for me. I have my 50th birthday coming up. And winning individual silver is pretty much the best present that I could imagine.”
Matt Hudson and Ava Jones combined to take silver in the barebow mixed team. Seeded at number two, the pair defeated Austria (150-136) and Denmark (152-141) before defeat to Russia (144-123). Ava Jones, making her World Archery 3D Championships debut, came in fourth in barebow women.
Other top 10 individual finishes came for Kim Timberlake (4th in longbow women), Joella Bates (8th in longbow women) and Lee Wilkins (10th in longbow men). Timberlake’s march to the bronze medal match included a 96-66 quarterfinals win over third seed Paula Virmasalo (FIN).

China represents just 3% of Walmart’s business. But the market is fast-growing—and in charge of that growth is Christina Zhu, the president and CEO of Walmart China.
Zhu is one of the execs featured on Fortune’s new Most Powerful Women Asia list , published today. She comes in at No. 19 for her role running a $24.6 billion business that has grown 19% year-over-year.
My colleague Nicholas Gordon writes about Zhu’s tenure in the role and Walmart’s history in China in a new feature . Walmart entered China in 1996. Today, its success comes from a few strategies to meet the high expectations of the Chinese shopper: extreme convenience, in the form of lightning-fast delivery, and an “in-person shopping experience so novel that stores have become vacation destinations for shoppers throughout the region.” In China, Sam’s Club is bigger than Walmart’s namesake retailer. Shoppers show up to buy in bulk items including gift boxes of mooncakes and abalone for the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Other execs who make this year’s MPW Asia list include repeat No. 1 Tan Su Shan, who leads the Singapore-based bank DBS Group and familiar faces like Canva’s Melanie Perkins and Huawei’s Meng Wanzhou, who all appeared on our 2026 global MPW list .

articles.title_orig: 800 people on one plane: what China’s giant flying wing could change forever
articles.title_zh: 800 people on one plane: what China’s giant flying wing could change forever
articles.source: Futura, le média qui explore le monde
articles.content_orig:
To fly fast, far, and as cheaply as possible while packing in the maximum number of passengers: that’s the economic magic airlines have been chasing for decades. Take the Airbus A380, for example. At its peak, Emirates managed to fit up to 615 passengers on one. Officially, this flying giant is certified for a jaw-dropping 853 people. That’s huge on paper—but in practice, it’s never happened. Why? Comfort, for one thing.
Now, a group of Chinese scientists want to get back to those stratospheric capacities with a new kind of plane that could carry up to 800 passengers. But here’s the most interesting twist: it’s not about returning to classic airliner shapes. Instead, the China Aerodynamics Research and Development Center (CARDC) is focusing on a flying wing design—picture something a little more UFO than cigar with wings. It ditches the traditional long fuselage, separate wings, and tail section in favor of a wide, blended shape.
Relying on a flying wing isn’t exactly breaking news, though the advantages are genuinely appealing. This design, with its elongated wings and cabin seamlessly merged into the wing structure, brings major perks:
So why aren’t airlines tripping over each other to put passengers in these futuristic behemoths? Well, for starters, they’d have to get rid of windows. And no, that’s not just a shame for sightseeing—it actually means reinforcing (and therefore weighing down) the structure. Cramming 800 people into a flying wing without windows? Good luck getting everyone a view! Even that alone is a deal-breaker for airlines, who can hardly imagine asking passengers to board windowless commercial planes.
Then there’s the size. The Chinese concept would be about 279 feet (85 meters) wide and 141 feet (43 meters) long. Sure, that’s five meters less in wingspan than an A380, and almost half as long, but this leads to another serious headache: airports would need major renovation to accommodate passenger boarding for such a massive aircraft.
And let’s not forget the logistical mountain of actually managing 800 passengers boarding a single plane. Even if a flying wing plane—currently still at the wind tunnel testing stage—has definite appeal, it’s safe to say the days of cigar-shaped aircraft with two wings aren’t over yet.
Meanwhile, the old payload giants like the A380 and the classic Jumbo jets have lost their edge. Today’s Airbus A350 can already carry nearly 480 passengers across the Atlantic on just two engines. That’s enough efficiency for airlines, and crucially, it doesn’t require a complete overhaul of airport infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.title_zh: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.content_orig:
The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.
Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response.
The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached.
The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement.
According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead.
Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme, former British ambassador to Israel, Matthew Gould, said any decision by the UK to expel Israeli diplomats would inflict "grievous damage" on the relationship between both countries.
He said areas affected could include defence, security and technology.
Gould told the programme: "When you've got to a stage where you are chucking out the big majority of Israeli diplomats in London, I don't think that's purely symbolic.
"I think at that point you're doing really quite serious damage to the structure and the substructure of the relationship."
He added that governments "have a choice", that the expulsion of Israeli diplomats would be a "gift to the Israeli right", and would help Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu win re-election.
France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them.
Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution."
She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it."
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close.
"It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month.

articles.title_orig: China's $100M Gaza Pledge: Beijing Hasn't Said What's Spent
articles.title_zh: China's $100M Gaza Pledge: Beijing Hasn't Said What's Spent
articles.content_orig:
Choose your language to begin.
Nine months after Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged $100 million to ease the crisis in Gaza, Beijing has not said how much of it has been spent. When Sun Zhen, who heads China’s diplomatic office to the Palestinians, announced new aid at a Sept. 29 reception in Ramallah — urgent cash support for the Palestinian Authority and three more tranches through UNICEF, the U.N. Development Programme and the Egyptian Red Crescent — he gave no amounts but said the details are still being coordinated.
Palestinian Economy Minister Mohammed Al-Amour attended on behalf of President Mahmoud Abbas. The Chinese office’s English readout said only that Sun “outlined China’s assistance to Palestine.” The details came from Palestinian media .
Sun highlighted that China, working with UNICEF, has already delivered winter clothing and medical supplies to more than 38,000 children in Gaza and medicines to six health facilities. That is a small share of Gaza’s roughly 1.1 million children, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics . China reported the Gaza deliveries by the number of people helped, not by cost, making a comparison between the $100 million pledge and other donors’ spending difficult.
The $100 million was always modest. In April 2025, the EU announced up to €1.6 billion ($1.8 billion) for the Palestinians over three years, including €620 million ($697 million) in grants to the Palestinian Authority.
All of that pales compared with Gaza’s immense need. A U.N. damage and needs assessment , released in April 2026, put the cost to rebuild and rehabilitate Gaza at $71.4 billion over the next decade.
China’s longer-term footprint is even smaller. MBN’s China Tracker monitors projects across the Middle East and North Africa under the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s global infrastructure and investment program. It records four in the Palestinian territories since 2023, all in or near Ramallah: a Chinese school, a Friendship Square, an 11-kilometer extension of Beijing Road, and the Friendship and Development Building signed this September, which Chinese officials call their largest aid project in Palestine.
“China’s primary interests in Gaza are currently political and strategic rather than commercial,” Mordechai Chaziza, an associate professor at Ashkelon Academic College in Israel who studies China’s role in the Middle East, told MBN via email. “Beijing seeks to strengthen its image as a supporter of the Palestinian cause, reinforce its role as an alternative diplomatic actor in the Middle East, and challenge the perception that the United States is the only external power capable of shaping regional outcomes.”
That approach also shows in reconstruction, where China has stood alone. On Sept. 23, the U.S.-backed Board of Peace, chaired by U.S. President Donald Trump and set up to oversee Gaza’s postwar rebuilding, unveiled a $2.45 billion , six-month plan of 66 projects. The board’s high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, said the plan depends on Hamas disarming.
China was invited to join the board in January, but it has not said whether it will, saying only that it backs a U.N.-centered system. Staying outside “may limit China’s direct influence over reconstruction decisions,” Chaziza said. But working through Egypt, Arab states and Palestinian institutions lets Beijing keep influence “while avoiding the political and financial risks associated with leading the reconstruction process.”
China’s presence is most concrete in supplies. MBN confirmed in U.N. records that the Chinese company Haike was awarded a standing U.N. supply agreement in April 2025 for mobile homes in Gaza. The agreement sets no quantity or value, so it guarantees no sales. The Israeli business paper Globes reported that Haike won the contract with a bid 50 to 60 percent below the runner-up, and that a Chinese firm was among the lowest bidders on a later U.N. Development Programme contract for 45,000 homes. MBN could not independently verify the bid figures.
Chinese companies have the technical capacity and experience to take part in Gaza’s reconstruction, Chaziza said, but how big a role they play “will depend less on economic capability and more on political arrangements.”
If reconstruction runs through “Western-backed institutions with strict procurement conditions, Chinese firms may face limitations,” he said. If Arab states and international organizations take a more inclusive approach, Chinese companies “could become important participants.”
The test is what comes next: whether the cash and the three tranches arrive, at what value, who wins the Gaza contracts and whether Beijing ever engages with the Board of Peace.
“China’s goal is not to replace the United States in Gaza,” Chaziza said, “but to expand its political influence by presenting itself as a supporter of Palestinian rights, a partner of Arab states, and a potential contributor to reconstruction while protecting its broader regional interests.”
Houda Elboukili contributed reporting

articles.title_zh: Trump’s Energy chief says truckers could see diesel relief within days after executive order
articles.content_orig:
Stuart Varney hosts an exclusive interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright to discuss President Donald Trump's order to lower diesel prices. Wright analyzes crude oil markets, high gas prices and the Colorado climate lawsuit.
Truckers could begin seeing relief from high diesel prices as soon as Saturday, Chris Wright said, after President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at temporarily expanding highway access to red-dyed diesel and providing relief from certain federal diesel-tax penalties and payments.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright joined FOX Business’ Stuart Varney on " Varney & Co. " to discuss the administration’s push to bring down diesel prices as tight global supplies continue to squeeze drivers and businesses.
President Donald Trump signs an executive order temporarily expanding access to red-dyed diesel for highway use. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Wright said truckers could begin seeing relief by Saturday, five days after Trump signed the order.
"The order was signed yesterday, and it's five days for Treasury and the Department of War to find the specific authorizations."
Trump’s order directs the Treasury Department to determine within five days whether it can defer certain federal diesel excise-tax payments. It also directs the IRS to provide penalty relief for dyed diesel sold for highway use or used on highways through Dec. 31, while federal agencies work with states and industry to expand access.
TRUMP OPENS RED-DYED DIESEL TO TRUCKERS IN BID TO SLASH FUEL COSTS
Wright pointed to disruptions abroad as a key source of the pressure, citing Russia, China and reduced flows of refined products from the Middle East.
Stuart Varney highlights President Donald Trump's new executive order waiving restrictions on red dye diesel for highway use. The policy aims to lower fuel costs for truck drivers across the United States.
"We're in a crisis right now with a shortage of diesel because of a conflict between Russia and Ukraine , China deciding not to export diesel anymore, and we still have reduced flows of refined products out of the Middle East, although they're on their way up," Wright said.

Despite the tight market, Wright said he believes the worst of the price spike may have already passed.

"I think diesel prices peaked a couple weeks ago. They're down 20, 25 cents already. I suspect we see a gradual decrease in diesel prices in the coming weeks and months ahead," Wright said.

articles.title_orig: The Email She’d Been Waiting For
articles.title_zh: The Email She’d Been Waiting For
articles.content_orig:
The Colorado State freshman had spent years working her way through New Zealand’s youth national system, hoping for an opportunity to represent her country on the world stage. Now, just weeks into her first preseason with the Rams, the opportunity was in front of her.
While typically a call, O’Brien received an email of New Zealand's roster for the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland.
“Usually we'll get an email saying, “hey, you'll get called in a week,” but we just got the straight email. I was scrolling, scrolling, scrolling. I was like, “Oh my gosh,” when I saw my name,” O’Brien said. “My best friend, who's at Xavier, she also made it and we've known each other since we were 10. It was amazing.”
Although not her typical way of being selected for a roster, it became even more special when she found her best friend of more than a decade, Penny Brill, would be joining her on the squad.
O’Brien made a quick call home followed by a message to Colorado State coach Keeley Hagen.
“I called my mom and my dad first and then I messaged Keeley, which was so exciting because she knew that I was nervous and didn't know fully, 100% if I was going,” O’Brien said. “So that was a really special moment.”
One of the highest honors awarded to a young female soccer player, this was an opportunity she built throughout her childhood. Her selection was the culmination of years spent developing with New Zealand's youth system.
O’Brien represented New Zealand at the U-17 and U-19 levels. However, after attending a camp in the U-17s, O’Brien tore a ligament in her ankle, making her unavailable just before the 2024 World Cup.
This setback did not end her World Cup ambitions as O'Brien later made New Zealand’s U-20 squad, joining them for the competition qualifier in Tahiti in 2025.
New Zealand won the Oceania tournament, securing its place in the 2026 World Cup and giving O’Brien the opportunity she had been working toward.
“That gave us qualification for the World Cup winning that, and then we were drawn in a pool, a very hard pool,” O’Brien said. “We had America, Italy, and Japan, which is basically the pool of death. But we were super excited; such a cool opportunity to play such high-class teams.”
Following the qualifier, O’Brien and the Kiwis faced off twice against Australia in a preparatory series in late May, building momentum ahead of the World Cup. Both games came up a draw, using the time for coaches to look at the quad and players to get a feel of what they might encounter in Poland. For O’Brien, it gave her more than the opportunity to wear her country’s kit, it gave her the confidence she needed to compete at a higher level and test herself.
The timing of the selection came at an unusual juncture for O’Brien. She had just begun to settle in at CSU when she learned she would soon have to leave for Poland.
As a true freshman living in the dorms, O’Brien was navigating life in a new country, a new idea of school, and the demands of a collegiate soccer player. Her new roommate and teammate, Fabienne Bos, became one of the people sharing the experience with her.
Bos remembered O’Brien discussing the possibility of making the New Zealand roster, knowing how much the opportunity meant.
“She was telling me about the World Cup coming up and she was pretty confident about making the team,” Bos said. “But of course it's always a scary, scary moment because she really wants to make it. When she made it, she was just very happy.”
Not only did O’Brien receive lots of support from her new roommate, but also from CSU’s coaching staff. They helped O’Brien prepare for the differences between an American college game and New Zealand's national system.
New Zealand’s play looks a little different than out in the West, focusing mostly on defense, something that the Rams were going to have to prepare O’Brien to face.
“Keeley and the whole team were obviously so excited for me and wanted to prepare me in the best way possible and have such a high standard of training,” O’Brien said. “I played fullback for a bit, which was helping me prepare because we play a 3-5-2 for our country, it's a little bit more defensive. Getting some experience there was really helpful before I went. Keeley did that for me, which was amazing.”
O’Brien’s journey to the World Cup was not one she made alone. CSU’s coaching staff worked to help her meet the demands of a new game.
Through on and off field training, CSU staff helped to shape O’Brien’s natural skills into something she could use anywhere.
“I sat down and went over some film with her because they were obviously really focused on the defensive side. I tell all our players, we're a resource here to help you,” Hagen said. “That was obviously unique and awesome for Poppy, and we try to help her in every way, training being one of them, film being another thing. So that's what we did.”
With much preparation from staff, O’Brien left with support which gave an opportunity to enter the World Cup more familiar with her national team’s demands.
Before the tournament began, the team faced off in a friendly against South Korea in a scoreless draw and eventually winning the penalty shootout 5-4. Additionally, the Kiwis played a professional club in Poland, using the games to prepare for the speed and physicality of World Cup competition.
“We had that time together to prepare and get back as a team after not being together for a while,” O’Brien said. “So that was really beneficial, and then straight into it, basically”
New Zealand started tournament play against Japan on Sept. 5 in Lódz, Poland. Japan dominated a scoreless first half and opened the second with a quick goal off a header from close range. New Zealand’s Lily Brazendale equalized the game only 10 minutes later with an easy tap.
The Kiwis ultimately fell 2-1 after Japan capitalized on a late penalty, breaking the stubborn New Zealand defense. The loss set the tone for a difficult group stage against three powerful opponents. New Zealand faced Italy on Sept. 9, losing 3-0, before meeting the United States on Sept.12 in a 9-0 defeat.
Although not scoring herself, O’Brien played in all three games providing New Zealand with depth and pace.
The result left New Zealand tied for 22nd place with New Caledonia and Costa Rica. Despite the losses, the Kiwis and O’Brien were grateful for the opportunity to show up on such a large stage. With 54 teams and some of the best players in the world, O’Brien still looked to the bright side.
“No matter what, I feel like representing your country is such an honor and such a pride. Compared to that U-20 level, it's just that one step up of excitement,” O’Brien said. “Playing against mostly pro players is super cool. The game's that much more physical and that much more technical, just learning so much was awesome as well.”
This experience on an international stage gave O’Brien a chance to measure herself against elite competition and take lessons back to CSU.
After the results in Poland, O’Brien still had something left unfinished and people who waited for her return. Her selection allowed her to play in Colorado State’s first two matches of the season, but it was a month before she would be a Ram again, reemerging in the lineup against Wyoming on Sept. 17. She has since started the past three matches.
Her time away from CSU had not separated her from the Rams, as her team continued to support her throughout the tournament, even catching her game against the US. Through check-ins and encouragement, the Rams showed that no matter the outcome, she still had family back in the States.
“I’m super honored for her to have that. It's the highest privilege that you can have to represent your home team; just so happy that she got that experience,” Hagen said. “We let her go and gave her what she needed. The team supported her, texted her, just tried to encourage her every step of the way.”
One of these teammates waiting to support her was her roommate.

articles.title_orig: Cornell brings in ex-Justice official Sally Yates to review school’s handling of sex assault claims
articles.title_zh: Cornell brings in ex-Justice official Sally Yates to review school’s handling of sex assault claims
articles.content_orig:
School trustees appoint Sally Yates to review policies as university grapples with fallout from alleged frat gang rape
A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced on Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration , will spearhead the review, the trustees said. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the adequacy of campus police responses, and more.
“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” the trustee chair, Anne Meinig Smalling, said in a statement.
The announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.
Yates will look at how the woman’s complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.
The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by the Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation that Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.
The lawsuit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.
New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter – the review that Yates now will lead.
Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza on Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.
Yates had a decades-long career at the justice department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.
She achieved particular prominence in January 2017, when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed justice department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.
Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.
Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the justice department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.
She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.

articles.title_orig: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.title_zh: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.content_orig:
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.
"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."
"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
Students chant slogans during a demonstration against under-resourced schools, in Paris, Tuesday. Teresa Suarez/AP hide caption
The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.

articles.title_orig: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.title_zh: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.content_orig:
Rising rent puts an end to the dim sum and Sichuan restaurant that has been in the neighborhood for almost 15 years.
Mama Ji’s (opens in new tab) in the Castro was filled with diners Monday night. Waiters bustled around, moving between the compact dining room and sidewalk tables, shuttling plates of kung pao shrimp, triple “C” wings, and hot-and-numbing fish. They told diners about the night’s special, inspired by the most recent trip Lily Ji — customers know her as Mama Ji — took to the Sichuan province of China: crispy lotus-root cake topped with minced pork in fish sauce.
Judging by how busy the restaurant was, you’d never guess it would likely be diners’ final visits. The last day of service for Mama Ji’s, which opened almost 15 years ago, is set for Oct. 31.
Ji and her husband, Marv Wolpa, posted a letter on the door sharing the news and expressing gratitude for the neighbors who have supported their mom-and-pop restaurant but saying it is time for them to put their time and energy into their personal lives. “Work is a lot; I won’t miss the work,” Ji said. “But I will miss the people.”
In an interview with The Standard, Ji gave more context to the closure: The landlord had raised the rent, citing rising insurance costs and an inability to charge more for the residential unit above Mama Ji’s. “I said, ‘Whatever that’s your decision,’” Ji said. “That’s my decision to not continue.”
The couple, who are Castro residents, started serving the food Ji grew up eating as a pop-up, then transitioned to the full restaurant in 2013. Over the decade and a half the couple served their neighborhood, Mama Ji’s became a staple of the neighborhood.
One couple dining Monday night expressed their sadness. The waiter repeated what the letter said, noting that Ji and Wolpa are ready to retire. “All things in the world must end,” he concluded as he walked away.
As for Ji, she didn’t miss a beat when asked about what she plans to do next: “Relax!”
Madeline Taub is a food reporter intern at The Standard. She was previously a contributor to Cityside’s food publication, East Bay Nosh. She graduated from UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.

Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director at Chanel . “I am happy with where we are at.”
Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. In Vanity Fair’s list of the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.
Blazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.
One of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featured Vanessa Paradis in a birdcage ; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.
After several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.
The same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.
after newsletter promotion
On his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”
The famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.

articles.title_zh: Brendan Carr’s ABC license fight meets a skeptical judge
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Editorial decisions at ABC News are being influenced by the Federal Communications Commission’s early license review of its TV stations, the network’s legal team told a U.S. District Court judge Tuesday.
The Disney-owned network is seeking a restraining order to stop the FCC’s action, which its attorneys said was unprecedented and an attempt by the Trump White House to chill free speech.
Disney attorney Beth Wilkinson said the FCC’s action is having an impact on ABC News coverage in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, as the network tries to avoid further action from the agency that regulates over-the-air broadcast TV licenses.
“We are making different editorial decisions,” Wilkinson said during the court hearing in Washington. “We are watching everything that we do because every time we do something — even not broadcasting this presidential speech — brings out the anger in the administration and the retaliation from the agency.”
Wilkinson was referring to President Trump’s frustration over ABC’s decision not to air his July 16 speech about voter fraud. The network chose to run it on its news streaming platform. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr criticized the move and said it would be considered in the license renewal process.
Wilkinson cited Carr’s complaint as an example of how the review is being driven by Trump’s unhappiness over the network’s coverage across its news programs, its late-night show “Jimmy Kimmel Live” and its topical daytime chat show “The View.” The FCC’s action, she said, is the administration “retaliating with their government power against ABC’s right to protected speech.”
Assistant U.S. Attorney Dimitar P. Georgiev argued for the FCC that ABC is trying to avoid the commission’s regulatory process by taking the case to the U.S. District Court. Georgiev said the license renewal was initiated because of a dispute over documents in the commission’s investigation into alleged discriminatory hiring practices at Disney.
Judge Loren L. AliKhan did not issue a ruling. She asked the FCC to provide further documentation on its claim. Disney will have until Oct. 14 to respond.
Trump has frequently threatened to have TV station licenses pulled when he believes he is treated unfairly on news and talk programs. He has also successfully extracted multimillion-dollar settlements from CBS and ABC after suing the networks over news content he believed treated him unfairly.
The Nicaraguan-born commentator has been the most ubiquitous Republican critic of President Trump on ‘The View,’ CNN’s ‘NewsNight’ and a new digital offering ‘Bleep! With Ana Navarro.’
ABC is the first network to take the FCC to court over the threats.
Wilkinson noted that Carr said during a visit to Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida that “broadcasters that are running hoaxes and news distortions, also known as fake news, have a chance now to correct course before their license renewals come up.”
The licenses for eight ABC-owned TV stations, including KABC in Los Angeles, were originally scheduled for renewal between 2028 and 2031.
Carr has said ABC’s daily talk show “The View” should not be exempt from the FCC’s equal time rule that requires broadcasters to bring on opposing candidates to provide balanced coverage. Wilkinson noted that the program — which was given the exemption in 2002 — has avoided using clips of politicians during its popular “Hot Topics” segment at the top of the program.
Carr also said earlier this year that stations could be subject to discipline if they “don’t operate in the public interest” after criticisms from the White House about coverage of the Iran war .
Carr called for the ABC license review in April, days after Kimmel delivered gags about the White House Correspondents’ Dinner attended by Trump for the first time as president and described first lady Melania Trump as having a “glow like an expectant widow.”
The satirical remarks drew criticism after a man breached security at the Washington Hilton event while armed with a shotgun, handgun and several knives. The dinner was cut short and rescheduled.

articles.title_orig: Europe’s moment of supreme confidence
articles.title_zh: Europe’s moment of supreme confidence
articles.content_orig:
As global alliances shift and economic competition intensifies, Europe is responding with deeper integration, large-scale investment and renewed confidence in its industrial and technological strengths
If there is one key takeaway from the recent Munich Security Conference, it is a message of trust and confidence in Europe. The EU is a technology, trade and industry powerhouse. Around Europe, the signs of this strength abound: off the northern coast of Poland, just beyond the horizon, 233 giant turbines – each almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower – are about to rise from the sea floor. With German rotors, foundations designed in Denmark, and cables from Poland and Greece, they will be towering symbols of European manufacturing excellence and industrial might. As the latest additions to an already vast Baltic fleet, they are creating thousands of jobs across the supply chain; and when they are operational, they will supply an additional 5.5 million households with clean energy.
Producing energy made in Europe, by Europe, for Europe, Poland’s offshore wind farms are as important strategically as they are economically. They add to a buildout of clean power that is happening across the continent from Italy in the South to Ireland and Lithuania in the North. Cables and interconnectors – enough to wrap the Earth many times over – are being laid to link the windy northern seas with the sunlit Mediterranean coastline, creating a superhighway for the age of electrons.
An investment revolution is underway Meanwhile, cutting-edge fibre-optic sensors pioneered by Dutch innovators will be watching over the seabed to protect Europe’s critical infrastructure. New constellations of satellites developed in Belgium will offer enhanced surveillance capabilities from space, alongside cutting-edge radar systems from France and Spain. And all these systems will be connected by AI-powered 6G networks developed in Finland.
These are just a few of the nearly 900 investment projects financed by the European Investment Bank Group last year alone ( see Fig 1 ). By leveraging EU budget guarantees to mobilise private investment, the EIB Group is powering the unfolding energy and technological revolutions. The transition into tomorrow’s world is already in full swing in Europe – a major development that remains overlooked amid rapid geopolitical change. In fact, the overall investment in the EU’s energy transition reached a new record in 2025, approaching €400bn – from hydropower in Austria to new railways in Czechia, and from energy efficiency upgrades by small businesses in Croatia to clean technologies deployed by heavy industries in Portugal. Just in the past year, the combined market capitalisation of European renewables companies has risen by over 50 percent. Something that many thought impossible in the near term is already happening – Europe is irreversibly weaning itself off Russian gas.
European investments in defence are increasing even more rapidly. European defence stocks have tripled in value in the past three years. Europe’s industrial production capacity now exceeds even that of the US in critical areas, including artillery shells. Europe is moving by leaps and bounds into strategic sectors and technologies such as drones.
A new venture-capital ecosystem geared toward pioneering security and defence enterprises has emerged almost overnight and essentially from scratch.
A continent reshaped by disruption We have seen a similar mobilisation before. In 2020, no one expected that a European biotech company would pioneer a vaccine against an unknown virus in a matter of months, helping the world defeat a once-in-a-century pandemic. Nor did anyone think that European leaders would launch a massive recovery and resilience programme financed by joint debt – an unprecedented show of solidarity and unity. When Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine caused a massive spike in energy prices, everyone assumed that the European economy would buckle. Instead, the eurozone’s GDP grew faster than China and the US that year.
In the face of trade warfare, intense market volatility, and shifting traditional partnerships and alliances, European companies have proven resilient, not only diversifying their trade flows but also maintaining strong growth and investment. European stock markets ended up outperforming US exchanges in 2025, rewarding investors who put their trust in our economy. Unemployment is hovering near record lows, and growth is picking up – thanks to high-performing countries such as Spain and Poland. Europe has emerged as a beacon of stability in an uncertain world.
Time and again, the EU has adapted and reinvented itself in the face of crises, leaving it well prepared to navigate a tempestuous geopolitical environment. An export powerhouse, the EU is home to world-class universities and research centres, as well as a vibrant start-up ecosystem. Opinion polls show record levels of public support for the EU and the euro, and global surveys indicate that majorities around the world see the EU as a great power on an equal footing with the US and China.
European stock markets ended up outperforming US exchanges in 2025
They are right to do so. With a $22trn economy, a vast single market of nearly a half-billion people, and plans for another wave of enlargement, Europe’s weight in the world is undeniable. It may be a different kind of superpower, one that prizes values, rules, and multilateralism over sheer might. But its power lies in its commitment to principles and willingness to back its partners and allies, as demonstrated by its status as the biggest source of financial and military assistance to Ukraine.
Europe continues to build bridges in a world of walls. It is the world’s leading trade power, residing at the centre of a vast, ever-expanding network of free-trade agreements. It is also an investment superpower that promotes shared prosperity around the world. As the biggest source of humanitarian aid and development finance, Europe funds everything from global vaccination campaigns to projects to improve water supplies in Amman and Karachi. We do so because we remain committed to the same values that brought us this far. European unification started nearly eight decades ago from the ashes of two world wars. Our parents and grandparents learned from the tragedies and mistakes of that dark era, and we can draw inspiration from their example to shape a better future for ourselves and others around the world. Ours is a society based on inclusion, equality of opportunity, intellectual freedom, peace, and the rule of law.
We know what needs to be done to preserve this way of life. We need even deeper integration, including our capital markets. We need even more large-scale investment in critical infrastructure and strategic capabilities. We need simplification to make the EU more agile and efficient. And we need more win-win partnerships and alliances to diversify our supply chains and open new markets for our goods. Momentum is building in all these areas. European leaders’ minds are focused, and we are determined to capitalise on Europe’s strengths as the world’s underappreciated superpower.

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.

articles.content_orig:
Global Communications Director
The Government of Indonesia has announced that it will stop any further expansion of the Food and Energy Estates project in Papua and will shift all future development for the project for food and crops for bioenergy to degraded lands – a globally significant win for Indonesia’s nature, the climate, and local communities.
In twin announcements at the Indonesian Sustainability Forum in Jakarta, President Prabowo’s brother Hashim Djojohadikusumo, in his role as Special Envoy for Climate and Energy and the President’s Special Envoy for Multilateralism & International Trade Mari Pangestu said that Indonesia would shift both the rice and sugarcane projects to degraded land.
Mighty Earth Founder and CEO Glenn Hurowitz commented:
“President Prabowo and the Indonesian government have made a globally significant decision for people, nature and climate today by ending deforestation for its food and energy development. This decision renews Indonesia’s leadership in showing how to expand agriculture while protecting nature.”
“Mighty Earth and allies will be closely monitoring implementation, and supporting work with local communities in Papua to heal the damage that’s been done. We are hopeful about the potential of this decision to drive a continued shift to protecting and restoring nature and to sustainable agriculture.”
“This decision creates an opportunity for large-scale investments in achieving President Prabowo’s goal of restoring 12 million hectares of forest, peat, and other ecosystems. It’s a program of truly enormous significance that could provide habitat to endangered species and suck gigatons of carbon out of the atmosphere. We call on all friends of Indonesia to support this program. This decision means that Indonesia can fully achieve its potential to become a nature and climate superpower.”

03:19:00 – Rice and Energy Project Announcement by Ibu Mari Pangestu, Special Envoy of the President for Multilateralism & International Trade.
Excerpt from President Prabowo’s Special Envoy Hashim Djojohadikusumo speech:
“I’d like to make a major announcement. Now, because of our success in reaching rice self-sufficiency, the Government of Indonesia would like to announce especially by the Minister of Agriculture through me the Special Envoy, that the Ministry of Agriculture and the Government feels at the moment that it does not need to expand the further cultivation of rice in so-called forest areas.
The so-called 2-million-hectare food estate program is a program that we have already achieved without even planting 2 million hectares. We will embark and continue on intensification measures, using new breeds, new seeds, superior breeds of rice and soybeans to achieve that. So, I’d like to again reiterate the fact that the government sees no further need for expanding rice cultivation areas in the so-called forest areas and forest zones that were announced a few years ago…”

“I just want to repeat a very important message from Pak Hashim this morning…He basically said that because we have been committed Because we have been quite successful meaning that the 2 million hectares that were announced for food production are no longer needed. And he told me he forgot to say it and he asked me to add this message, is that, to, to have increased food and and biofuel production, moving forward, we will be using degraded land…
The missing part of that message is…We have over 12 million hectares of degraded land that can be used, for this, and the minute, and he asked me to say on his behalf that He did discuss this already with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry, and they agreed that any future production of food or biofuel production will be using degraded land, and it is part of the forestry ministry program of afforestation, reforestation, and revegetation.”

articles.title_orig: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return
articles.title_zh: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has confirmed its ‌‌first Ebola case after the death of a Kenyan national in Nairobi, who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The patient, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, had been ill for about a month before travelling by road from the DRC to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, and then flying to ⁠⁠Nairobi on Saturday, Aden Duale, Kenya’s health secretary, told a news conference on Tuesday.
Seeking to halt local transmission, Kenya’s President William Ruto said at least eight family members of the victim and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined, as he ordered an enhanced response to contain the virus in the country.
Earlier, Health Secretary Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced.
Patrick Amoth, director-general of the Kenyan Ministry of Health, said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released if they test negative for the virus.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.
The outbreak has claimed more than 4,000 lives, according to figures released by the government on Friday, and confirmed cases have ⁠⁠reached 8,300 across seven provinces, making it the worst Ebola epidemic in the country’s history .
The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “ far from over ” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
At the same time, the United Nations organisation has advised against imposing travel and trade restrictions on Kenya, DRC and Uganda following the Ebola-related death in Kenya.

articles.title_orig: Dr. Stein on Real-World Data, Targeted Combinations, and Immunotherapy in AML
articles.title_zh: Dr. Stein on Real-World Data, Targeted Combinations, and Immunotherapy in AML
articles.content_orig:
Eytan M. Stein, MD, explains how real-world data complements AML trials and where targeted agent combinations and immunotherapy research must go next.
Eytan M. Stein, MD, explains why real-world data matters in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). He also discusses how combining targeted agents could drive the next wave of progress, and why immunotherapy has yet to succeed in myeloid disease the way it has in multiple myeloma and lymphoma.
Stein, a hematologist/oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, begins with the limits of clinical trial data. Trials have strict entry criteria and often exclude patients with abnormal kidney, liver, or cardiac function. As a result, trial results reflect a selected population that may be healthier than patients treated in routine practice. They need to be interpreted in light of who was actually enrolled.
Real-world data, which is often retrospective, looks at what happens to patients treated outside of trials who may not have met every eligibility criterion. According to Stein, these analyses show how a drug may perform once it is used in a broader population.
He also points to racial disparities as a key reason this evidence matters. In the United States, underrepresented minorities are under-enrolled in many clinical trials, and real-world analyses help show how therapies work in those populations. Taken together, retrospective data can confirm primary trial findings. It can also give physicians confidence that a drug will work not only for a relatively fit clinical-trial patient, but for patients who may not be as healthy.
Turning to treatment, Stein highlights the targeted agents developed over the past 10 to 15 years. He identifies combination strategies as the area where significant advances are likely. Targeted agents now exist for IDH, FLT3, and NPM1 mutations, yet some patients with newly diagnosed AML carry all 3. That raises open questions. Should these patients receive chemotherapy with 3 targeted agents or with 1, and which targeted agent is best? Stein asks whether AML will follow the path of multiple myeloma, where combining many drugs has become a way to cure patients or bring them to a curative transplant, or whether a different approach will emerge.
Stein also addresses immunotherapy in AML, an area where he says there has not yet been substantial progress. Bone marrow transplant is itself a form of immunologic therapy, but apart from transplant, immune-based treatments have not been successful in AML. This contrasts with multiple myeloma and lymphoma, and he notes how much survival has improved in multiple myeloma over the past 15 years. He emphasizes the need to understand why immunotherapies are not working in myeloid leukemia, so that approaches can be developed to make them successful.
